# Joints

## Summary

Joints are structures in the <u>musculoskeletal system</u> that regulate the type and <u>range of motion</u> between two or more adjacent bones, enabling body parts to move harmoniously. They can be grouped according to their structure (synovial, <u>cartilaginous</u>, and <u>fibrous joints</u>) or their degree of mobility (<u>diarthroses</u> and <u>synarthroses</u>). <u>Diarthroses</u> (<u>synovial joints</u>) are freely movable and consist of elements (e.g., <u>intraarticular space</u>, <u>synovial fluid</u>, <u>joint capsule</u>) that allow low-friction movements between opposing articular surfaces and supporting structures (e.g., <u>ligaments</u>, <u>menisci</u>, <u>articular discs</u>). The range and axes of motion of a <u>synovial joint</u> are determined by the shape of its constituent parts. Examples of <u>synovial joints</u> include <u>hinge joints</u>, <u>saddle joints</u>, <u>plane joints</u>, and <u>ball and socket joints</u>. <u>Synarthroses</u> (<u>fibrous joints</u>) are immovable and connected by thick <u>connective tissue</u>. Depending on the type of tissue connecting the articular surfaces, <u>synarthroses</u> are further classified into four types: <u>syndesmoses</u>, <u>synchondroses</u>, <u>symphyses</u>, and <u>synostoses</u>.
